Tech Scan: Workflows & factories

How do you turn an agreed requirement into a reviewable change without giving an agent authority to release it?

Draft research reference; not locally deployed or benchmarked. Vendor documentation describes capabilities, not proof that this composition works in your environment. Issue 64 is a research proposal, not local validation.

On this page
Choose the work and outcomeBuild the AWS-first candidateEnforce the boundariesTest before adoptionSources

Choose the work and outcome

A workflow arranges activities, dependencies and decisions: for example, a product owner and engineer agree acceptance criteria, review a design and break it into tasks. A software factory, as used here, assembles the intake, agent execution, tests and review handoff that can turn an issue into a pull request (PR). It is a composition, not a guarantee of correctness or an approval to deploy. Do not confuse this with AWS AI Factories, which is managed on-premises AI infrastructure for training and inference, not an issue-to-PR service.[10]

AWS has no managed software factory: no AWS product takes a GitHub issue to a reviewed pull request out of the box. The closest managed option is Kiro Web, which runs a task in an isolated cloud sandbox and opens a pull request for review, but never merges on its own. Kiro Web is a paid-plan feature; in autonomous mode it selects the model automatically, so it cannot pin a named model for a Bedrock-only policy. Confirm the current plan, region and data terms with Kiro before adopting it.[10][11]

Before choosing tools, the product owner records the user need, acceptance criteria and constraints. The engineering lead records the repository, required tests, permitted data and model, operating owner and who may approve the change and release. An unresolved mandatory requirement stops the pilot; AWS preference does not override a hard gate.

Kiro specs offer requirements (or bug analysis), design and tasks documents; Quick Spec can generate these without approval gates, so select and verify the review process rather than assuming every mode pauses.[1] For a team whose existing coding agent has a supported integration, GitHub Spec Kit is an alternative: its documented flow runs constitution, specify, clarify, plan, checklist, tasks, analyze, implement and converge, with the checklist, analyze and converge steps as quality gates. GitHub Copilot is the documented default integration. Spec Kit's shell steps run with local user privileges and no capability sandbox, so a specification workflow is not a sandbox.[2] Compare the artefacts against your own acceptance criteria; neither format proves the work is correct.

Track the work where the code and pull requests live: GitHub Issues with GitHub Projects, or GitLab issues, is the default. Keep Jira where the team already uses it; the handoff shape is the same. Linear works the same way only when a human or orchestrator delegates each issue to one agent. Never let agents claim work from a shared queue themselves: when several agents race for the same issue, work is duplicated or silently overwritten. Assign each issue to one agent or one human owner instead.[10]

Related decisions: Agents chooses the worker; Harness explains the agent loop; Sandbox covers execution isolation.

Build the AWS-first candidate

For a GitHub repository and an approved Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, trial the Claude Code GitHub Action as a component in an owned issue-to-PR workflow. Its use_bedrock: "true" option supports Bedrock with OpenID Connect (OIDC); its configuration documents a named provider model. OIDC also requires separately configured AWS trust, credentials and GitHub id-token: write permission; the option alone does not set these up.[3][4] Condition the role's trust policy on the repository, branch or environment, not only on the AWS account, so a token minted elsewhere cannot assume the role.[14] The action also supports Vertex AI and Foundry providers; use_bedrock is a choice among providers, not the only OIDC route.[3] This is not a complete factory: the team must build and test intake, authorisation, PR creation, independent checks and the handoff. It does not establish that all execution, logs or data remain in AWS.

  1. The product owner and engineer approve a bounded issue, requirements and expected tests; an authorised operator assigns it to one run.
  2. The platform engineer pins the action to a reviewed commit, configures a narrowly scoped AWS OIDC role and selects an approved Bedrock model and region. Use an isolated, ephemeral GitHub-hosted runner, or a just-in-time self-hosted runner, with restricted network and credentials; do not give the agent production access.
  3. The runner checks out a controlled base, generates a branch and proposed change, and opens a PR. CI independently runs the required tests; the PR records the issue, model, action revision, test results and unresolved risks.
  4. A qualified human reviews the diff and evidence. Only an authorised human merges; a separate authorised human release decision follows the applicable deployment process.

Hard gates: confirm required capability, approved data location and retention for every provider and log, identity and authorisation, model and API availability, execution and network boundaries, and an accountable operator. Record each decision and evidence. If any gate fails or is unknown, stop; seek an approved exception or select another route.

Assessed alternatives: the Claude Code Action is not the only issue-to-PR service. Each of the following was assessed in the research proposal; confirm the current plan, region and data terms with the vendor before trialling any of them.[10]

Issue-to-PR alternatives assessed in the research proposal
ProductIssue-to-PR flowWhen it fits
Copilot cloud agentAssign an issue to Copilot inside GitHub; it opens a draft pull request.Teams already on GitHub Copilot that want the factory inside GitHub.
Codex CloudCloud tasks from the Codex app; results land as a pull request.Teams already using Codex that want managed cloud execution.
Cursor Cloud AgentsAssign tasks to cloud agents from Cursor; they open pull requests.Teams already using Cursor that want cloud agents on the same model route.
OpenHandsSelf-hosted, open-source agent; bring your own key.Teams that must host the factory themselves and supply their own model key.
DevinManaged agent service; assigns work from issues and opens pull requests.Teams that want a managed service and accept a third-party vendor in the loop.
Factory DroidsManaged droids that take issues and open pull requests.Teams that want a managed factory without building the runner and controls.
GitHub Agent HQPlatform layer for comparing providers' pull requests.Teams comparing several agent providers; not a factory on its own.

Conditional alternative: use Kiro specs when its review workflow and data/model settings pass those same gates. If policy requires a named model, configure model access management, exclude Auto and choose an approved default; verify inference location and actual routing before use.[9] Use Spec Kit when the team needs a supported existing agent and a separate specification flow. A different hosted factory is a research option only after its data, identity, model, execution and retention terms are approved; do not infer Bedrock routing from an AWS brand.

Enforce the boundaries

Issue text, repository files, tool output and third-party skills can contain untrusted instructions. A prompt such as “do not deploy” or an AGENTS.md rule guides behaviour; it is not an enforcement boundary. Do not combine untrusted issue or fork input, shell execution, a write token and secrets in one privileged job. Limit tokens, isolate jobs and pin reviewed dependencies.[7] Review skill instructions and scripts, pin them by commit, disable automatic updates and reject skills that fetch remote instructions at runtime.

  • Merge: configure protected branches or rulesets to require independent CI status checks and human review. Protect workflow files, instructions and CODEOWNERS with code-owner review; keep the agent and its app off bypass lists. Test these settings rather than relying on a self-reported agent test. Any one listed owner can approve, and GitHub reads CODEOWNERS from the base branch, so list owners who can review the change, not only the author.[5][6]
  • Deploy: a merge must not substitute for release approval: a merge can trigger deployment immediately unless a separate gate is configured. Where supported and configured, GitHub environments can require a reviewer and restrict deployment branches; prevent self-review where appropriate, and separately verify that the release approver is not the merger; self-review prevention alone does not establish this. Check plan and repository availability, and restrict administrator bypass where available and prevent other deployment paths from bypassing the gate.[8]
  • Action inputs: keep restrict_untrusted_prs at its default true, so the action denies code-running commands on pull requests from authors without write access. Never set allowed_non_write_users to "*": it bypasses the action's security checks, and the action's own documentation warns against it except for workflows with very limited permissions.[3]
  • Execution: restrict filesystem access, egress, credentials and duration outside the prompt. Isolation reduces risk but does not prove the model or generated code is safe; see the Sandbox reference.

Keep deployment secrets beyond the agent's write boundary

Do not expose organisation-wide or repository-level deployment secrets to untrusted issue-to-PR execution. Where GitHub Actions is used, place sensitive deployment material in protected environments with configured approval and branch restrictions where the plan supports them, and bind the job to that environment; the existence of an environment name is not a protection rule. Prefer scoped AWS OIDC role credentials rather than stored AWS access keys. Restrict the OIDC trust relationship to the intended repository, ref or environment, and ensure the agent cannot edit the workflow or policy that grants access. [15] [16]

In the pilot, try reading a deployment secret from the agent's authoring job, editing the release workflow to widen access, requesting credentials under an unapproved ref and deploying without the environment reviewer. Record the expected denial and the actual enforcement point for every path. Review job logs and produced artefacts for leaked values; masking alone is not exfiltration protection.

Test before adoption

For checks and review evidence, see Verification; for the release handoff, see Delivery.

The platform engineer and security reviewer should run a non-production pilot against an approved test repository. Record the exact action revision, runner image, model, region, permissions and expected and observed results. Try an injected issue, a secret in a diff, a failing test, and a change to a protected workflow or CODEOWNERS file. Attempt a merge with a failing check and with the agent identity; both should be denied under the proposed policy. Also attempt a command from an untrusted pull request; it should be denied while restrict_untrusted_prs is true.

Record the PR, logs, costs, failures and remaining gaps. The designated owner decides whether the evidence meets the agreed gates; a passing pilot is not production authorisation. Test the actual deployment approval path separately. No local pilot, independent benchmark or representative reader study supports this draft yet.

Credential gate: a working issue-to-PR loop is not accepted until an untrusted authoring runner cannot retrieve protected deployment credentials or gain production authority via a changed workflow. Test the action identity and all alternate deployment paths, not just the primary pipeline.

Choose the next autonomy level, not the highest one

Factory maturity is an engineering decision about ownership, handoffs, independent checks and recovery. Kiro Crew's team reports 1,000 PRs merged in a week and describes five stages; the number is an author-reported throughput result, not an independent benchmark of acceptance quality or a goal for other teams. Use the stages below as a diagnostic for the bottleneck you have measured, not a recommendation to run more agents. [17]

StageHuman and agent responsibilityWhat must hold before progressing
1. One sessionDeveloper directs a bounded task and reviews the resultReproducible task, controlled tools, test evidence and a stop limit
2. Several sessionsDeveloper coordinates parallel changesSeparate working trees, clear task ownership and conflict handling
3. Durable context and scheduled workSessions resume work using reviewed records and time triggersProvenance, memory scope, expiry, budget and stop or cancellation path
4. Defined agent pipelineDistinct stages hand off through a queue and recorded evidenceIndependent checks, explicit state transitions and retry safety
5. Agent coordinating sessionsPerson owns intent and material decisions; the coordinator assigns and observes workHost-enforced permissions, immutable action trail, incident response and human approval for high-impact operations

Entry rule at every stage: require a durable task and action record, bounded per-agent identity and permissions, a named memory owner and independent quality gates. More merged PRs do not establish better user outcomes, fewer defects or permission safety. Start with one recurring, reversible task; progress only after its failure handling and evidence are satisfactory. [18]

Do not adopt a closing factory

Do not build a factory on a product whose vendor has ended support. Use the replacement named in each row.

Closing factories and their replacements
ProductStatusUse instead
Amazon Q Developer for GitHubSupport ends 30 January 2027; new installations stop 18 November 2026.Kiro and the Kiro GitHub App.[12]
Google JulesRead-only since 11 November 2026; winds down 31 December 2026.Google Antigravity, or an agent in Coding agents & coordination.[13]
Amazon CodeCatalystClosed to new customers; maintenance only.GitHub with the Claude Code Action, or Kiro Web.[10]
SWE-agentSuperseded; no longer the recommended issue-to-PR agent.The AWS-first candidate in Build the AWS-first candidate.[10]
SweepShut down.The AWS-first candidate in Build the AWS-first candidate.[10]
Roo Code and ContinueShut down or read-only since June 2026.A supported editor agent in Coding agents & coordination.[10]
AiderStalled; no active development.A supported editor agent in Coding agents & coordination.[10]
Bedrock Agents ClassicMaintenance mode; closed to new customers 30 July 2026.Bedrock AgentCore.[10]

Gaps and open questions

The alternatives above are summarised from the research proposal; confirm the current plan, region and data terms with the vendor before trialling any of them.[10]

Kiro Web's availability date and region are not stated on its primary page; confirm both with Kiro before adopting it.[11]

Re-check the model tiers and AgentCore availability after re:Invent (29 November–4 December 2026).
